items.label: section_header
items.text: BASES

items.label: text
items.text: We saw in Chapter 16 that bases are substances that neutralise acids by combining with the hydrogen ions in them to produce water. When we are referring to a base at this level, we usually mean a metal oxide, a metal hydroxide or ammonia.

items.label: text
items.text: Metal oxides, such as copper(ll) oxide and magnesium oxide, are bases.

items.label: text
items.text: The copper(ll) oxide (black powder) reacts with hot dilute sulfuric acid to produce a blue solution of copper(ll) sulfate.

items.text: BASES AND ALKALIS

items.label: text
items.text: Some metal oxides are soluble in water and react with it to form solutions of metal hydroxides, for example:

items.label: formula
items.text: N a _ { 2 } O ( s ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \rightarrow 2 N a O H ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: All the Group 1 oxides do this reaction, so for potassium oxide we would get:

items.label: formula
items.text: K _ { 2 } O ( s ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \rightarrow 2 K O H ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: Most other metal oxides are not soluble in water.

items.label: text
items.text: Calcium oxide dissolves slightly to form calcium hydroxide:

items.label: formula
items.text: C a O ( s ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \rightarrow C a ( O H ) _ { 2 } ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: Another alkali you will meet is a solution of ammonia (NH). The ammonia reacts with the water to form ammonium ions and hydroxide ions:

items.label: formula
items.text: N H _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } O ( 1 ) \rightleftharpoons N H _ { 4 } + ( a q ) + O H ( a q )

items.label: text
items.text: All these solutions contain hydroxide ions. We learned in the last chapter that we can define alkalis as solutions that are a source of hydroxide (OH-) ions, so all of these solutions are alkalis.
